stories.headline: Update: Supreme Court Allows Trump Voter-Citizenship Database, Blocks Missouri GOP Map on Same Day
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court issued two significant election-related rulings Friday, less than six weeks before the midterm elections. In an emergency order, the court's majority allowed the Trump administration to proceed with using the Department of Homeland Security's SAVE database to check state voter rolls for potential noncitizens, overriding lower court blocks. Voting rights groups warn the system could incorrectly flag eligible voters and suppress turnout in competitive states.

In a separate ruling the same day, the high court again blocked Missouri Republicans from using their preferred 7-1 congressional map, ordering the state to revert to an older district design. The decision is a blow to the GOP, which had fought to use the more favorable map ahead of November.

The twin rulings illustrate the court's outsized role in shaping the mechanics of the 2026 midterms. Conservatives praised the SAVE database decision as a necessary safeguard against noncitizen voting, while critics — including former White House ethics lawyer Norm Eisen — urged against overreacting, noting the ruling is temporary and legal challenges continue.

The decisions come as the administration faces broader legal battles over election rules, including Democratic lawsuits over the deployment of federal agents to polling sites and ongoing disputes over voter registration backlogs in Texas.

stories.headline: Update: Trump and Xi Conclude Washington Summit; Xi Pledges Two More Meetings This Year
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up their three-day Washington summit Friday with a visit to the National Archives to view historic documents before Xi's departure. Trump confirmed he will meet Xi again in November and at least once more before year's end, describing the summit as having produced 'great strides,' though observers noted a relative scarcity of concrete policy outcomes.

The trade truce between the two countries was extended from November to January — shorter than the year-long extension Beijing had sought. Key disputes over tariffs, rare earth supplies, and U.S. chip access to China were deferred to further negotiations. On Taiwan, Xi reiterated opposition to U.S. arms sales, while Trump has not publicly responded; U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is 'no change' in U.S. Taiwan policy.

Some Republican senators publicly criticized the summit's lavish treatment of Xi, warning against red-carpet diplomacy with a strategic rival amid domestic economic pressures and an unpopular Iran war. Former Defense Secretary Leon Panetta described the visit as delivering 'an awful lot of pomp, but not a lot of substance.'

The summit concluded as both sides continue to navigate tensions over artificial intelligence governance, with the leaders discussing the issue but producing no public agreement on safeguards or joint frameworks.

stories.headline: Update: Mississippi Police: Black Woman Found Hanging From Tree Was Dead Before Body Was Staged
stories.summary:
Police in Jackson, Mississippi, said Friday in court that Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black mother of four whose body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in August, was already dead before her body was placed there. A detective testified that investigators believe the scene was staged and that her death was related to a drug dispute. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide.

Fortune's mother told reporters outside the Jackson Police Department that the coroner informed her the death was not an actual hanging and that her daughter was dead before being placed in the tree. Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are Black. A third suspect, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in Friday and was charged with murder; a hearing is scheduled for Monday.

The August discovery had sparked widespread fear and grief in Jackson, a majority-Black city with a deep history of racial violence and lynchings, prompting weeks of public demands for answers. The new court disclosure that the hanging was staged significantly alters the nature of the case, though it does not diminish public concern over a pattern of such incidents nationally.

Rep. Ayanna Pressley has cited at least 10 documented incidents of Black Americans found hanging in recent years in a September letter to Congress signed by more than 50 lawmakers, calling for federal investigation of all such deaths.

stories.headline: Trump's Triumphal Arch Moves Closer to Construction as Federal Advisory Panel Ends Historic Preservation Talks
stories.summary:
A federal advisory council terminated required consultations Friday over President Trump's planned 250-foot 'Triumphal Arch' near Arlington National Cemetery, clearing a procedural hurdle toward construction after local historic preservation officers refused to sign off on harm-mitigation plans. The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, said it would submit a final report next month, and a Democratic congressman reported that excavation work has already begun on the site.

The arch, proposed for a site roughly four miles from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drew fresh criticism this week after Trump announced it would also serve as a military facility capable of deploying snipers and drones from its roof and plaza. Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth called the dual-use plan 'foolhardy' in a letter to the Pentagon and FAA, warning of airspace safety risks near a runway approach path that was the site of a deadly 2025 midair collision.

The FAA ruled last week that the structure would not pose a flight risk, but opponents in Congress and among historic preservation advocates continue to contest the project on multiple grounds, including its potential effects on 42 nearby historic properties. The council's termination of talks does not require agreement between federal and local officials, allowing the project to proceed despite unresolved objections.

The arch has become a flashpoint in broader debates over presidential monument-building and the use of public funds for what critics call vanity projects. Supporters argue it will serve as a symbol of American strength and military capability.

stories.headline: FBI Hack Exposes Medical Records and Personal Data of Up to 60,000 Agents
stories.summary:
Cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims to have breached FBI systems, stealing sensitive fitness-for-work medical records — including blood and urine test results, doctors' notes, home addresses, badge numbers, and spousal information — for tens of thousands of current and former special agents. The group now claims to hold data on roughly 60,000 FBI personnel, far more than the 38,000 initially estimated. The FBI acknowledged the breach Wednesday and said it is "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

The stolen records are particularly alarming because some reportedly identify agents involved in investigations related to Russia, China, and drug cartels, raising counterintelligence concerns. Security experts warn the data could enable phishing, blackmail, identity fraud, or physical targeting of law enforcement personnel. Professor Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, described the breach as "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."

Unusually, ShinyHunters is not demanding money. Instead, the group is seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May that it claims offended them. Samples of the data shared with journalists appeared genuine and included senior officials such as deputy directors.

Experts stress that unlike stolen passwords, medical records cannot be reset, meaning the compromise is permanent. Reports from 404 Media suggest details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed in the breach.

stories.headline: Russian Drone Kills Seven in Kyiv, Strikes Data Centre as Russia Widens Infrastructure Attacks
stories.summary:
A Russian drone struck a business centre in Kyiv on Friday that housed a major data centre, killing four people and injuring dozens more. A separate overnight attack killed a 14-year-old boy whom Israel's foreign ministry identified as an Israeli citizen. Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the overnight strikes killed seven people in total and injured 59 across the city.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia has systematically widened its campaign to target data centres and internet providers, disrupting connectivity for ordinary Ukrainians. About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region suffered internet outages earlier this week due to strikes. Electronic information boards in the north-western city of Lutsk also went dark, with officials attributing the outage to Kyiv data centre damage.

Russia's defence ministry confirmed it struck the Datagroup facility, claiming it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence. Some firms have begun relocating data from damaged servers to facilities abroad. Ukraine's foreign minister called the attacks on data centres an attempt to disrupt "life-saving" missile and drone alert systems that protect civilians.

Zelensky said additional decisions were made at a Friday security meeting to protect data centres and critical communications infrastructure. His defence technology adviser acknowledged potential local disruptions but stressed Ukraine's decentralised internet architecture would prevent a nationwide outage.

stories.headline: Man Shot at 2024 Trump Butler Rally Dies More Than Two Years After Assassination Attempt
stories.summary:
Jim Copenhaver, 76, a U.S. Army veteran who was shot twice at Donald Trump's July 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died from complications related to his injuries, the Pennsylvania attorney general confirmed. Copenhaver died Wednesday at a Pittsburgh hospital. The Allegheny County medical examiner issued a statement confirming the death.

Copenhaver was struck in the arm and the abdomen during the attack. A bullet remained lodged near his spine as recently as last year, forcing him to walk with a cane. He and fellow shooting victim David Dutch had sued the federal government in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries. Another rally attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed on the day of the shooting; the gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service.

Trump posted a tribute to Copenhaver on Truth Social, calling him a "true American patriot" and referencing the attempted assassination: "A crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values." House Republicans also paid tribute on Friday.

Copenhaver's death elevates the confirmed death toll from the Butler shooting to two attendees, more than two years after the event that became a defining moment of the 2024 presidential campaign.

stories.headline: ICE Raids on Meatpacking Plants Alarm Beef Industry, Raise Consumer Price Fears
stories.summary:
Immigration enforcement actions targeting meatpacking operations in Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas have drawn protests from cattle industry groups and two Republican senators, who say the raids are disrupting operations in a sector heavily reliant on immigrant labor. The complaints put agricultural-state Republicans in tension with the Trump administration's broader enforcement agenda.

Industry representatives warn that workforce disruptions at processing facilities could reduce throughput and drive up beef prices for consumers, compounding existing inflation pressures. The concerns come as the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland has flagged rising inflation anxiety, and traders now price in a 71 percent likelihood of a Fed rate hike at next month's meeting, up from 55 percent a week ago.

Proponents of the enforcement actions, including immigration hawks within the administration, argue that the operations are necessary to enforce federal law and that employers in the meatpacking sector have long exploited undocumented workers. The administration has not publicly commented on the specific industry objections raised by Republican lawmakers.

The story underscores a recurring fault line within the Republican coalition between immigration hardliners and agriculture-state members whose constituents depend on immigrant labor. With beef prices already elevated, the political and economic stakes of continued enforcement in rural processing communities are drawing national attention.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Proposes Seven-Day Deal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz at UN Sidelines
stories.summary:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi privately detailed a new proposal Thursday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York: the United States would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observe a ceasefire including Lebanon — in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks within seven days. The proposal was conveyed to U.S. officials through mediators and closely resembles the June Memorandum of Understanding that collapsed when Iran resumed attacks on shipping.

The White House said Friday that U.S. officials are having "positive and constructive conversations" with mediators and described itself as facilitating significant oil exports through the strait. However, Saudi Arabia was reported to be skeptical of the latest push, according to a person familiar with private deliberations. Trump has previously said he is in no rush to reach a deal despite high oil prices fueling inflation.

Analysts note the accelerated timetable may reflect mutual economic pressure — Iran faces punishing sanctions while elevated oil prices are straining the U.S. economy ahead of November midterms. Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute said Araghchi suggested a speedy deal could benefit Trump politically, but cautioned that "deep suspicion" remains on both sides, particularly around whether Iran is buying time to ease its economic pain rather than offering a durable settlement.

A significant obstacle remains on the Iranian side: hard-liners who dominate the security forces may resist compromises championed by moderate President Masoud Pezeshkian. Iran's UN mission made no immediate comment on the proposal. In a sign of diplomatic movement, Pezeshkian hosted Qatar's prime minister Friday, with Doha serving as a key mediator between Washington and Tehran.

stories.headline: German Students Strike Nationwide Against Possible Return of Compulsory Military Service
stories.summary:
School strikes erupted across Germany on Friday, with demonstrations in Hamburg, Berlin, Frankfurt, Kiel and more than a hundred other cities, as students protested the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. The immediate trigger was a wave of official medical exam invitations sent to 18-year-old men who had indicated no interest in joining the Bundeswehr on government questionnaires — a step protesters said amounted to a backdoor path to conscription.

A voluntary military service law took effect in January under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has made rebuilding Germany's armed forces a centerpiece of his government in response to Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine and U.S. pressure to increase European defense contributions. The law allows the Bundestag to move toward compulsory service if security conditions worsen or volunteer numbers fall short. The Defense Ministry confirmed that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical exam applies to all men born after December 31, 2007, regardless of whether they expressed interest in service.

Protesters, many of them 16 and 17 years old, carried banners reading "We won't take part in your wars" and vowed to continue striking until compulsory service is taken off the table. Organizer Bela Breitner said the government is "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service" and that young people are not willing to accept it passively. Germany currently has approximately 186,700 troops and aims to reach 260,000 by the early 2030s — numbers that voluntary recruitment alone is unlikely to achieve.

The protests reflect a broader tension in Europe between governments seeking to rearm in response to Russian aggression and younger generations who grew up in a post-Cold War security environment. Germany abolished compulsory military service in 2011 under Angela Merkel. Friday's nationwide strikes represent the most visible domestic pushback yet against Merz's defense agenda.

stories.headline: Kazakhstan Detains Five Senior Military Officials After 14 Soldiers Drown in Caspian Sea Exercise
stories.summary:
Five senior Kazakh military officials have been detained following the deaths of 14 service members who were swept into the Caspian Sea during a military exercise Thursday. The soldiers were among 17 who fell into the water while disembarking from a boat approximately 43 kilometers from the city of Aktau in southwestern Kazakhstan. Officials said the incident occurred during a combat training mission amid a sudden deterioration in weather conditions and rising winds; three survivors were rescued.

Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They face suspicion of criminal negligence. An interior ministry committee has been established to investigate whether safety requirements were observed, whether weather conditions were properly assessed, and whether the technical specifications of the boat were adequate.

The deaths occurred during the Caspian Defense 2026 exercise, which involved more than 500 military personnel, warships, and coastal units. Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov confirmed a pretrial investigation is underway. The swift detention of senior officers signals that Kazakh authorities are treating the incident as a serious failure of command rather than an unavoidable accident.

stories.headline: Trump Rules Out Bessent as AI Czar, Leaving 'Super Intelligence' Role Unfilled
stories.summary:
President Trump said Friday he is ruling out Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent as his artificial intelligence czar, posting on Truth Social that Bessent will not serve as the "Super Intelligence (SI) Czar" — Trump's proposed rebrand of the AI policy role. The statement appeared to be a direct response to a Semafor report that had listed Bessent as a top contender for the new position.

The White House has been working to establish a dedicated AI leadership role as competition with China over artificial intelligence intensifies and calls for regulation grow from industry leaders and foreign governments. Trump's "Super Intelligence" rebranding signals a shift in how the administration is framing U.S. AI policy, though no alternative candidate for the czar position was named Friday.

The announcement comes amid a week of intense global focus on AI governance, with OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs warning the UN Security Council of existential risks, Pope Leo XIV cautioning against machines eroding humanity, and the Trump-Xi summit touching on AI safeguards without producing concrete agreements. The identity of the eventual AI czar is expected to shape U.S. regulatory posture and international negotiations on the technology for years ahead.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Says Trump Gave Final Approval for Ukraine to Produce Patriot Missiles
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced Friday that President Trump has verbally confirmed Ukraine will receive a license to domestically produce Patriot air defense missiles, describing "concrete agreements" reached on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York earlier this week. Zelensky posted the news online, saying the two leaders met and that Washington has now given the go-ahead for a weapons production arrangement Kyiv has pursued for months.

The Patriot missile system is among the most effective air defense platforms Ukraine has deployed against Russian strikes on its cities and infrastructure. Domestic production rights would give Ukraine the ability to sustain and expand its air defense capacity without depending entirely on U.S. or allied stockpile transfers, which have at times been delayed or constrained by political disagreements in Washington.

The announcement marks a significant shift if confirmed formally, as the Trump administration has sent mixed signals on the depth of its military support for Ukraine while simultaneously pushing for a negotiated settlement with Russia. Secretary of State Rubio has previously noted Ukrainian strikes on U.S.-linked assets as a complicating factor in the relationship. No formal White House confirmation or official documentation of the license approval had been released at time of publication.

The development comes amid broader diplomatic activity surrounding the U.N. General Assembly, where Ukraine, the United States, and Russia have all been engaged in parallel diplomatic maneuvering over a potential ceasefire framework involving energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping corridors.

stories.headline: Bill Gates Warns AI Is Powerful Enough to Cause 'a Billion Deaths,' Calls for Regulation
stories.summary:
Bill Gates, in remarks set to air on NBC's "Meet the Press" this weekend, warned that artificial intelligence is "certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths," marking one of the starkest public statements yet from one of the technology industry's most prominent long-term optimists. Gates also called on lawmakers in Washington to regulate AI development, aligning himself with a growing chorus of voices in the tech sector urging government intervention.

The comments represent a notable escalation in Gates's tone on AI risk. While he has previously acknowledged dangers, his prior public posture on AI has been broadly optimistic, emphasizing its potential to accelerate medical breakthroughs and economic development in poorer countries. The shift comes weeks after the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic appeared before the U.N. Security Council to warn of existential AI risks and urge global safety standards.

Gates's warning lands in the middle of an active policy debate in Washington and internationally over how to govern advanced AI systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published an essay calling for slowing AI development for safety reasons, and a senior Anthropic safety researcher has publicly placed the probability of AI-caused human extinction at greater than 10 percent. The Trump administration has thus far taken a deregulatory posture toward AI, rolling back Biden-era executive orders on AI safety.

The remarks are likely to intensify pressure on Congress and the White House to articulate a coherent regulatory framework, though there remains deep disagreement between those who favor strict guardrails and those who argue heavy regulation would cede AI leadership to China and other competitors.

stories.headline: U.S. Government Backs Elon Musk's Legal Fight Against €120 Million EU Fine on X
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice filed an application with the EU's General Court on Thursday seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge against a €120 million fine levied by the European Commission against X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter. The fine, issued in December 2025, found that X deceived users by selling blue verification checkmarks without meaningfully verifying the identities behind accounts, in violation of the EU's Digital Services Act.

U.S. Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate argued that the European Commission had "inappropriately attempted" to extend its regulatory reach over American companies. The DOJ contended that the U.S. has a legitimate interest in the case to ensure any ruling is consistent with how territorial jurisdiction is understood under international law and does not harm U.S.-headquartered digital services that contribute significantly to the American economy.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed the EU action in sweeping terms, calling it "an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments" and declaring that "the days of censoring Americans online are over." Musk reposted Rubio's remarks on X with the comment "absolutely." The European Commission responded that it is "ready to defend" its position, saying it has a "solid case" based on the DSA and is not targeting any specific nationality but simply enforcing its digital and democratic standards.

The U.S. intervention marks an unusually direct assertion of government power in support of a private company owned by a politically connected billionaire, and is likely to intensify already strained U.S.-EU relations over technology regulation. The case is the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act, a landmark regulatory framework that has increasingly put Brussels at odds with American tech companies and, now, the U.S. government itself.

stories.headline: Germany Investigates 105-Year-Old Alleged Nazi POW Camp Guard for Accessory to Murder
stories.summary:
German prosecutors have opened an investigation into a 105-year-old man suspected of serving as a guard at Stalag 326 VI K, a Nazi prisoner of war camp in Senne, northwestern Germany, on allegations of accessory to multiple counts of murder during World War Two. The Dortmund public prosecutor's office confirmed the case Friday, noting that a second former guard at the same camp had also been under investigation but died several months ago at the age of 99.

Stalag 326 was one of the largest POW camps in Nazi Germany. One in three Soviet prisoners of war who entered German captivity between 1941 and 1945 passed through the Senne complex, according to the site's memorial organization. Of the 180,000 to 200,000 Soviet soldiers registered there, tens of thousands died and are buried at the site; prisoners also faced forced labor, extreme malnutrition, and brutal mistreatment. POWs from France, Poland, Serbia, and Belgium were also held at Senne.

The case underscores the acute difficulty Germany faces in prosecuting Nazi-era crimes more than 80 years after the war's end. Germany abolished the statute of limitations for murder and accessory to murder in 1979 specifically to keep such prosecutions legally viable, but the near-total death of surviving perpetrators and witnesses makes convictions increasingly rare. A 101-year-old guard from another camp was sentenced to five years in 2022 but died while appealing his conviction and never served time.

A third centenarian, a former guard at the Hemer Stalag VI A camp, is also reportedly under separate investigation. German prosecutors have continued to pursue these cases as a matter of legal principle and historical accountability, even when the likelihood of a completed trial and sentence is diminished by the defendants' extreme age.

stories.headline: Italy Bans Burqa and Niqab in Schools, Caps Non-Italian-Speaking Pupils at 30 Percent
stories.summary:
The Italian government approved a decree Thursday banning the burqa and niqab in schools and imposing a 30 percent cap on pupils with little or no Italian-language ability in the first year of primary, middle, and high school. The hijab, which leaves the face visible, is not covered by the ban. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni framed the measures as tools of integration rather than division, stating that no tradition should compel a young woman to hide her face.

Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara described the language cap as purely linguistic rather than a citizenship restriction, arguing it would prevent the formation of what he called 'ghetto classes.' Local school offices will be required to distribute pupils with limited Italian more evenly among nearby schools, with exemptions permitted where redistribution is not possible and supplementary Italian instruction offered.

Opposition parties accused the Meloni government of pandering to the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party ahead of a general election next year. Critics argue the measures stigmatize immigrant communities rather than supporting genuine integration. The decree takes effect immediately but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.

Non-Italian citizens currently make up 11.6 percent of pupils in Italy's schools. A 2010 ministerial notice had previously set a 30 percent guideline on non-citizen pupils, but the new decree enshrines the limit in law for the first time, significantly strengthening its enforcement.

stories.headline: Jay-Z Rape Accuser Files Formal Retraction, Says Allegation Was Entirely False
stories.summary:
A woman who sued Jay-Z and Sean 'Diddy' Combs in 2024, claiming she was drugged and raped at age 13 after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000, has filed a formal declaration stating the allegation was untrue. In a court filing made Thursday, she wrote that Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter 'never raped me,' that she had never met or spoken to him, and that her claims against both Carter and Combs were false. She also stated she received no money or threats from Carter or anyone acting on his behalf.

The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, dropped her original lawsuit in February 2025. Carter subsequently sued her and her attorneys, led by lawyer Tony Buzbee. In Thursday's declaration, filed in connection with that lawsuit, she said she had not authorized the filing of the original complaint and that Buzbee and other lawyers filed it 'without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence.'

Buzbee, in a statement to Rolling Stone, said he had not seen the new declaration and noted that multiple lawyers heard the same account from the woman before he became involved. Carter has maintained the original allegations were a 'blackmail attempt' and described them as 'frivolous, fictitious and appalling.' The woman has now been removed as a defendant from Carter's ongoing lawsuit against her former legal team.

The case drew widespread attention given Carter's prominence and its connection to the broader criminal proceedings against Combs. Carter, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said in February 2025 that the trauma his family endured 'can never be dismissed.'

stories.headline: New Jersey Governor Demands Lieutenant Governor's Resignation After Ethics Investigation
stories.summary:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell a deadline of Friday to resign after a law firm hired by her office concluded he had committed repeated violations of the state's ethics and anti-discrimination policies. Investigators found Caldwell had twice attempted to obtain state employment for his girlfriend, made inappropriate advances toward a staffer's acquaintance, and engaged in other conduct that persisted despite multiple warnings and mandatory training.

Sherrill stated that Caldwell's 'ethical lapses persisted despite multiple warnings and trainings' and described the violations as 'serious and repeated.' The findings were published Wednesday, and Sherrill publicly called for his resignation Thursday, setting a firm deadline one day out.

Caldwell, a Democrat, has not yet publicly announced whether he will comply with the governor's demand. The situation is politically significant because Sherrill, who took office this year, is now confronting a misconduct matter within her own administration at an early stage of her governorship.

The story has drawn coverage from outlets across the political spectrum, including Fox News, NBC, The Guardian, and The Hill, reflecting the bipartisan interest in an intra-party accountability dispute involving senior state officials.

stories.headline: Germany Approves €2.5 Billion Fuel-Tax Cut as Consumer Prices Surge
stories.summary:
German lawmakers approved a temporary fuel-tax relief package worth €2.5 billion, equivalent to approximately $2.8 billion, set to take effect next week. The measure was backed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing coalition as part of an effort to ease rising energy costs on consumers and businesses amid continued pressure on household budgets.

The relief package represents one of the more significant near-term fiscal interventions by the Merz government since it took office, targeting pump prices directly at a time when fuel costs have weighed on European consumers across multiple sectors. No end date for the temporary relief was immediately detailed in available reporting.

Germany's economy has faced persistent headwinds including weak industrial output and elevated energy prices since the disruptions caused by the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The fuel-tax cut signals the coalition's willingness to use the federal budget to cushion consumers even as Germany debates longer-term fiscal constraints under its constitutional debt brake.

The vote adds Germany to a growing list of European governments that have introduced or extended fuel-tax relief mechanisms in 2026 in response to sustained price pressures.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Xi Summit Concludes With Trade Truce Extended, Key Disputes Unresolved
stories.summary:
President Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state dinner Thursday at the White House, marking Xi's first visit to Washington in more than a decade. The summit was heavy on pageantry — a pescatarian menu with sesame-crusted sea bass, a bald eagle sculpture gifted to Xi, and a guest list packed with tech billionaires including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman, and Jeff Bezos — but produced limited concrete agreements. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the two countries extended their tariff truce by two months, from November to January, falling well short of Beijing's reported hope for at least a year-long extension.

The thorniest issues separating the two powers — AI governance, Taiwan arms sales, rare earth supply chains, and the U.S.-Iran war — remained unresolved after the closed-door sessions. Xi called for cooperation to avoid the "Thucydides trap" of great-power conflict and reiterated that U.S. arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China. Trump has not publicly responded to Xi's Taiwan comments, though he faces bipartisan pressure to maintain support for the island. Xi also announced China would send two pandas to Zoo Atlanta as a gesture of goodwill.

The summit was shadowed by a parallel confrontation over press access. A federal judge ruled the Trump administration violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS Now, and Politico by banning them from the White House, and issued a temporary restraining order requiring their reinstatement. Despite the ruling, reporters from those outlets were initially denied entry to the state dinner before eventually being readmitted — prompting their lawyers to request an emergency hearing, alleging the administration had "repeatedly violated" the court's order.

The summit drew criticism from Republicans and Democrats alike. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis called the timing "bad" and analysts noted the lack of substantive breakthroughs despite elaborate diplomatic staging. Supporters of the summit argued that stabilizing the world's most consequential bilateral relationship — particularly amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran war and AI competition — was itself a meaningful accomplishment, even absent a landmark deal.

stories.headline: Update: Pakistan Strikes Afghanistan Again, Taliban Vows 'Appropriate Response'
stories.summary:
Pakistan launched a second wave of air strikes on Afghan territory in less than a week, hitting targets in Kandahar, Paktia, and Khost provinces, the Taliban government confirmed Thursday. The Taliban said four civilians were killed and others were wounded, with a provincial official reporting jets bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps in Paktia. Local eyewitnesses in Khost described residential areas being struck, with one saying "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel — there are only the homes of ordinary civilians."

Pakistan's government said its forces struck 10 targets in Afghanistan and characterized the operation as "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate," asserting the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to attempted attacks against Pakistan." Islamabad has accused the Taliban of harboring Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group that claimed a September 18 attack on a mosque at a police compound in northwestern Pakistan that killed at least 31 people. The Taliban denies sheltering the TTP, calling militancy Pakistan's internal problem.

Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid called the strikes "reckless, careless, and hostile" and warned they "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military," vowing an "appropriate response." Pakistan in turn cautioned that any further "provocative act" would be met with a response. The UN mission UNAMA confirmed at least three civilian casualties. The escalating cross-border strikes risk drawing two nuclear-armed neighbors — Pakistan and Afghanistan's de facto Taliban government — into a broader conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Trump FDA Nominee Overton Dodges Questions on Mifepristone Safety, Vaccines at Senate Hearing
stories.summary:
Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, appeared before a Senate committee Thursday for her confirmation hearing and largely sidestepped direct questions on two of the most politically charged issues before the agency: the safety of the abortion pill mifepristone and vaccine policy. Overton, a fierce opponent of abortion rights, declined to state whether she believes mifepristone is safe and effective, a drug that accounts for the majority of abortions in the United States and whose FDA approval has faced repeated legal challenges from anti-abortion groups.

The hearing put Overton in a difficult position between a Republican administration that has shown skepticism toward some public health orthodoxies and a Senate confirmation process that requires demonstrating basic scientific credibility. She did tell senators that the MMR vaccine is "safe and effective" — a position at odds with vaccine skeptics within Trump's orbit — but avoided many other pointed questions from lawmakers on both sides. Sen. Bernie Sanders pressed her on whether healthcare is a human right; she declined to give a yes-or-no answer.

The FDA commissioner's role is among the most consequential in federal public health administration, overseeing drug approvals, food safety, and medical device regulation affecting hundreds of millions of Americans. Supporters of Overton's nomination argue she will bring needed scrutiny to the agency's approval processes, while critics contend her record on abortion and science raises serious questions about her fitness to lead an agency whose credibility depends on scientific independence.

stories.headline: Texas Voter Registration Backlog Could Leave Thousands Unregistered Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
A system error in Texas has left tens of thousands of voter registration applications unprocessed for months, forcing county election officials to scramble to clear the backlog just weeks before early voting begins in the state's midterm elections. The Texas secretary of state's office alerted county election officials to the problem last week; it involves a technical issue with the Department of Public Safety's records system that delayed the processing of applications.

The error raises concerns that eligible voters who submitted applications in good faith could find themselves unable to vote if the backlog is not cleared before voter registration deadlines. Texas, which has some of the most restrictive voter registration rules in the country, does not allow same-day registration. County election officials are racing to manually review and process the delayed records before early voting opens next month.

The development adds to a broader set of election administration concerns playing out ahead of the November midterms, including disputes over voter roll maintenance, non-citizen voting investigations, and a California Supreme Court order requiring the return of more than 650,000 seized ballots. Texas election officials have not said how many applicants may ultimately be affected or whether the problem has been fully resolved.
